Background: Hallucination—the generation of factually incorrect, internally inconsistent, or ungrounded content—remains a major barrier to the safe deployment of large language models (LLMs), particularly in high-stakes domains. The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-source Large Language Models via the Kerimov-Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Most existing hallucination-detection methods rely on external knowledge bases, model fine-tuning, or cloud-based APIs, limiting their applicability for private or fully local inference environments.

Methods: We evaluated the Kerimov–Alekberli (KA) information-geometric framework as a real-time, inference-time hallucination detector across six open-source LLMs running locally on Apple M5 Silicon hardware using Ollama v0.23.2 with Q4_K_M quantisation. The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-source Large Language Models via the Kerimov-Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: The KA framework monitors the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between consecutive output distributions relative to a Fisher Information Metric (FIM)-derived threshold (τ = 0.065). The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-source Large Language Models via the Kerimov-Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: Hallucination events are identified through First-Passage Time (FPT) alarms triggered when generation trajectories depart from the stable Riemannian output manifold. The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-source Large Language Models via the Kerimov-Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: We evaluated 120 responses (6 models × 20 questions) using prompts drawn from three established hallucination benchmarks: HaluEval (14 questions spanning Fact, Confuse, Date, Num, and Trap categories), FEVER (4 adversarial fact-verification questions), and SimpleQA (2 factual-recall questions). The record for Hallucination Detection and Reduction in Open-source Large Language Models via the Kerimov-Alekberli Information-Geometric Framework: Empirical Evaluation on HaluEval, FEVER, and SimpleQA states in its own abstract: All prompts were classified as Hard difficulty and targeted known LLM failure modes including off-by-one numerical errors, geographical traps, and disputed-attribution confounds.

Results: The KA framework achieved a session-level hallucination detection sensitivity of 90.9% (20/22 hallucinated responses correctly flagged) with zero false positives among correct responses (0/98).
